connection: Every odd integer > 5 is a sum of three primes (Helfgott), an additive three-witness pointwise theorem (F01,F12,F21,F33); the proof combines circle method for n ≥ N₀ with explicit finite verification below (F23).
why: The explicit major/minor arc plus computation architecture is a credible template for joining ES's analytic estimates to its already enormous verification range.
first_step: Read Helfgott's major-arc lower bound and explicit minor-arc constants; ask whether a similarly explicit lower bound for R(p) could bridge the remaining finite interval.

title: Romanoff's theorem on prime plus powers of two
connection: A positive proportion of integers have form p+2^k, giving a positive-density witness subset (F05w,F30,F33), unlike ES's universal target (F01).
why: The almost-everywhere density mechanism may reveal which sieve or Fourier estimates fail when upgraded to every input.
first_step: Compare Romanoff's lower-density proof with the ES almost-all exceptional-set proof and identify whether a pointwise lower bound can survive for residue classes of p.
refs: unverified: Romanoff, Über einige Sätze der additiven Zahlentheorie (1934)

title: Erdős's covering argument for prime plus powers of two
connection: The complement of n=p+2^k is controlled by congruence covering phenomena, resembling ES's finite congruence cover (F03) and thin-family unions (F34).
why: Covering congruences are a direct combinatorial mechanism for proving either coverage or obstruction, relevant to ES's certificate-line cover.
first_step: Write the covering congruence system in the Erdős argument and test whether ES failed primes have a finite modular covering explanation.
refs: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950) 113–123

title: Crocker's prime plus two powers of two obstruction
connection: The equation p+2^a+2^b=n has an explicit exceptional/obstruction structure (F01,F08w,F30,F33), contrasting positive-density coverage with universal coverage.
why: Its classification of failures may offer a way to search for structured ES failure families rather than only aggregate counts.
first_step: Read Crocker's construction (check whether his non-represented integers form a sparse family like 2^{2^m}−1 rather than residue classes) and compare its mechanism with the ES residue cover modulo 840 and the failed (★) primes.
refs: R. Crocker, On the sum of a prime and of two powers of two, Pacific J. Math. 36 (1971) 103–107

title: Cramér–Maier matrix method for pointwise short intervals
connection: The matrix method extracts pointwise irregularities at polylogarithmic scales (F04w,F21,F37), sharing ES's delicate pointwise-versus-average issue (F05,F21).
why: It supplies a warning and a tool: organize many correlated residue-class counts in a matrix rather than infer pointwise behavior from a mean.
first_step: Build the analogous residue-class-by-C matrix for R(p) over a modest prime range and test whether Maier-style row/column discrepancies appear.
refs: unverified: Maier, Primes in short intervals (1985), Michigan Math. J.; Cramér conjecture

title: Zsigmondy's theorem and its finite exceptional list
connection: Every n>1 has a new prime divisor in a cyclotomic difference except explicit small cases (F01,F23); cyclotomic factorization gives a short witness (F32) and finite exceptions (F25).
why: This is a clean example where primitive-divisor algebra turns universal existence into a finite exceptional classification.
first_step: Check whether any ES parametrization yields a cyclotomic factor whose primitive divisor forces d≡−1 mod 4C; begin with 4Cp+1.
refs: unverified: Zsigmondy, Zur Theorie der Potenzreste (1892); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zsigmondy%27s_theorem

title: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier primitive divisors in Lucas sequences
connection: A uniform primitive-divisor theorem gives a short prime witness for each sufficiently large sequence index, with a finite explicit exception regime (F01,F25,F32).
why: The proof combines algebraic factorization and explicit bounds to force a prime divisor; this may be adaptable if ES's tied integer 4Cp+1 has controlled primitive factors.
first_step: Read the BHV primitive divisor definition and test whether primitive factors of 4Cp+1 can lie in the required residue class −1 mod 4C.
refs: unverified: Bilu, Hanrot, Voutier, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers (2001), J. reine angew. Math.

title: Congruent primes via Heegner and Monsky arguments
connection: The congruent-number property for primes in particular residue classes has pointwise arithmetic criteria (F01,F29,F31), and elliptic-curve descent converts the question into a local/global witness problem (F06,F07).
why: The descent and 2-Selmer computations could inspire an arithmetic obstruction or certificate for ES's surface family.
first_step: Check the exact prime congruence classes and descent construction in Monsky's result; compare the resulting 2-adic local conditions with ES's F29 split case.
